The estuary was never the same shape two days running. At dawn, when the mist hung low over the mudflats like wet wool, the water retreated so far that the ribs of an old coal barge, wrecked before the war, poked through the silt like the spine of a prehistoric whale. By two in the afternoon, the sea was back, licking at the stone foundations of the seawall, carrying with it the cold smell of deep salt and weed torn from the reefs five miles out.

Arthur knew the tides not by the calendar pinned behind the pantry door, but by the groan of the kitchen floorboards. When the Atlantic pushed hard against the mouth of the bay, the groundwater rose beneath the house, and the pine planks swelled, stiffening the latch on the cellar door.

He had lived in the toll-keeper’s cottage for twenty-four years, long after the road was rerouted across the new concrete span three miles inland. The county council had stopped paying him in the late nineties, but they had also forgotten to evict him. A clerk in an office with drop ceilings and flickering fluorescent tubes had likely filed a form under *Miscellaneous Easements* and left it to gather dust. Arthur did not mind. He paid for his paraffin and tea with the money he made mending outboard motors and winding the tall clock in the parish church tower once a week.

Every morning at first light, after the kettle had boiled and the first mug of bitter black tea was drunk, he took the ash walking stick from beside the boots and went down to walk the strandline. 

People assumed beachcombing was a romantic pursuit—ambergris, message bottles, brass compasses lost by Spanish galleons. In reality, it was an inventory of human carelessness: blue nylon rope tangled into nests so tight only a razor could part them; plastic bottle caps with teeth marks from gulls that had choked on them; faded laundry detergent jugs with Spanish or Norwegian labels; and lengths of gray drift-timber, light as balsa from months in the brine.

Yet today was different. The night had brought a nor’easter, the kind that shook the slates on the roof and made the chimney sing in three distinct keys. 

At the southern bend, where the currents collided against a spit of shingle called the Crow’s Bill, the water had carved a shelf into the gravel. There, half-buried beneath a heap of kelp that still glistened with sea-lice, lay something that did not belong to the modern drift.

It was an iron-banded chest no larger than a breadbox, its timber black with saturated rot. The metal straps were swollen with rust, flaking off in orange wafers as Arthur brushed away the weed. It had no lock, only a hasp that had corroded through until it gave way under the nudge of his walking stick.

Arthur knelt on the wet stones, the damp immediately soaking through the knees of his corduroys. He didn't hurry. When you reach seventy, hurry is an insult to the things that have taken their time to find you.

He eased the lid back. It did not creak; the wood was too waterlogged for sound. 

Inside, wrapped in oiled canvas that had miraculously held against decades—perhaps a century—of immersion, was a bundle of small, flat objects. When he peeled back the tarred cloth with numb fingers, he found thirty or forty slates, the kind schoolboys once used in parish schoolhouses, bound together with rot-resistant hemp twine.

He slipped one free from the stack. 

The slate had been inscribed with a steel stylus, scratching white grooves through the dark, fine-grained stone. It had not been washed away because it had been cut, not chalked.

*October 14, 1888. Wind WNW, gale force. The light at the Point was doused at midnight by spray breaking the lantern glass. We burnt three barrels of tallow on the gallery until dawn. Hands raw. No ships seen in distress, God be thanked.*

Arthur sat back on his heels. The wind off the bay bit his ears, but he didn't pull his collar up. 

He took out another slate.

*July 3, 1891. A calm like oil. Mackerel run so thick by the gut you could scoop them with an iron pot. Martha brought out the boy to see them. He laughed until he fell into the bilges. A good summer.*

And another:

*January 9, 1895. Ice in the basin two inches thick. The gulls are walking on the bay. Cut my thumb on the barrel hoop. Salt got in it. Martha says a man who fears a little salt shouldn't take wages from the King.*

They were the logs of the old lighthouse that had stood on the outer skerry before the automated buoy replaced it in 1912. The tower had been demolished with dynamite in the thirties—Arthur’s grandfather had watched the dust rise from the mainland—and the rubble had been swallowed by the Atlantic. But someone, perhaps the keeper himself, had packed his daily scratchings into an ammunition box and hidden them somewhere high, only for a hundred winters of frost to finally break the masonry and loose them into the surf.

Arthur held the cold slate in his hands. He could feel the small irregularities where the keeper’s hand had trembled—perhaps from cold, perhaps from the palsy of old age. These were not state papers. They were not destined for an archive in London or Edinburgh. They were the smallest unit of human survival: the note that says, *I was here, the weather was cold, my thumb hurt, but we kept the light on.*

He thought of his own small rooms: the radio on the sideboard that only caught the shipping forecast and the Gaelic service; the row of grease-stained manuals for two-stroke engines; the tea tin on the mantelpiece containing seventy-three buttons he had found on the shore over forty years, each one once sewn to a coat that had gone somewhere else.

The tide was turning now. The first thin sheet of gray water crept across the shingle, touching the hem of his boot.

Arthur carefully laid the slate back into the box and folded the stiff, tarred canvas over the top. He gathered the whole box into his arms. It was heavy, sodden, smelling of iron, sulfur, and very old rain.

He walked back along the shoreline toward the cottage. The chimney was smoking softly, the peat he had cut in August burning down to white ash. Behind him, the tide followed his boot-prints, filling each depression with smooth water until the sand was flat again, unmarked, waiting for whatever the night decided to abandon.
